readingInstruction: Read Judges 15:1-16:31. These chapters finish the story of Samson, from his revenge on the Philistines through Delilah and his death in the temple of Dagon. Read slowly through chapter 16, and watch for the quiet sentence in verse 20: “he did not know that the LORD had left him.”
settingTheScene: Samson’s wedding has ended in betrayal, and his violence against the Philistines escalates. In the stories you read today, he burns their fields with foxes, kills a thousand men with a donkey’s jawbone, carries off the gates of Gaza, and then falls in love with Delilah. The text is brutally honest about a man with enormous gifts and no self-control. Samson never leads Israel into freedom, and the Philistines are not defeated in his lifetime. But the story ends with a surprising prayer. The man who lived by his eyes is blinded, humbled, and finally turns to the LORD. His last act is a sacrifice that begins the work God promised.
observation: Samson burns the Philistines’ grain with three hundred foxes and torches (15:4-5).
The men of Judah, afraid of the Philistines, bind Samson and hand him over; the Spirit rushes upon him, and he kills a thousand with the jawbone of a donkey (15:9-15).
Thirsty, Samson cries out to the LORD, and God splits a hollow place so that water comes out (15:18-19).
He visits a prostitute in Gaza and carries off the city gates on his shoulders (16:1-3).
“He loved a woman in the Valley of Sorek, whose name was Delilah” (16:4).
Delilah pressures him day after day until “his soul was vexed to death,” and he tells her the secret of his hair (16:16-17).
“He did not know that the LORD had left him” (16:20). The Philistines gouge out his eyes and set him to grind at the mill.
Samson prays, “O Lord GOD, please remember me and please strengthen me only this once,” and pulls down the temple, killing more in his death than in his life (16:28-30).
interpretation:
Samson is a study in contradictions. He is the Spirit-empowered deliverer, and the Spirit comes on him again and again. And yet his life is marked by appetite, revenge, and carelessness. The text never excuses him. Chapter 15 shows his motives to be personal grudges: “As they did to me, so have I done to them.” He is not fighting a holy war for Israel. He is settling scores. Even when he is thirsty and cries out to God after a great victory, his prayer includes the complaint, “Shall I now die of thirst?” God still answers him with water. The mercy of God is bigger than Samson’s failings.

Chapter 16 tells the tragedy of Delilah. Samson goes to Gaza for a prostitute and then falls in love with a woman who is paid to betray him. The details of the story are almost comic, three times he lies about the secret of his strength and three times she tries it out. And yet he keeps flirting with danger. He is like a man playing with fire, convinced he will not be burned. When Delilah’s nagging wears him down, he tells her everything. The cutting of his hair is not magic. It is the final break of a Nazirite vow that he had long been violating. The real loss is described in verse 20: “he did not know that the LORD had left him.” This is one of the most chilling sentences in the Bible. He wakes up and says, “I will go out as at other times.” He assumes the power will be there. But it is gone.

The consequences are severe. The Philistines gouge out his eyes. The man who followed his eyes into sin is now blind. They put him in bronze shackles to grind at the mill, like an animal. And they celebrate in the temple of Dagon, praising their god for delivering Samson into their hands. This is the lowest point, because the name of the LORD is being mocked.

But the story has one more turn. Samson’s hair begins to grow. In the dark, he turns to prayer. The prayer is short, and it is the first time in the story he calls on God as “Lord GOD” with personal appeal, asking to be remembered. His request is for vengeance, but it is also for the vindication of God’s name. God answers. Samson pushes the pillars, and the temple falls. “So the dead whom he killed at his death were more than those he had killed during his life.”

Samson is not a model of holiness. But he is a sign of God’s grace. Hebrews 11:32 lists him among those commended for faith, which suggests that his last prayer was a genuine act of trust. The same grace reaches the worst of us. His story also points to a greater one: a Savior who is delivered to the enemy, bound, mocked, and who by his death destroys the power of those who hold his people captive. Jesus did what Samson only pictured.
connection: Samson’s story fits the pattern of Judges’ downward spiral. The Nazirite vow is in Numbers 6. The loss of the Spirit echoes Saul in 1 Samuel 16:14. The temple of Dagon appears again in 1 Samuel 5. Hebrews 11:32 includes Samson, and Matthew 27:35-44 shows Jesus mocked by his captors and conquering through death. Colossians 2:15 and Hebrews 2:14-15 describe Christ’s defeat of the powers through death.
application:
Take the warning of verse 20 seriously. Spiritual drift is often not dramatic. It happens in small compromises that dull our sensitivity until we do not notice that God’s presence has become faint. Ask yourself honestly: when did you last feel a sense of God’s nearness? What may have been dimming it?

Second, guard your eyes and your heart. Decide on one specific boundary this week that will protect you from a recurring temptation.

Third, take hope from Samson’s last prayer. No matter how far you have fallen, God hears the cry of a humbled heart. Return to him today.
prayerPrompts: Tell God where you are gifted yet careless.
Ask him to open your eyes to your own heart before the drift goes further.
Thank Jesus for remembering and saving you.
